Yellow-eared barbet Psilopogon australis hatchlings emerge at a remarkably small size, with a neonatal wet body mass of just 3.8 grams [Ww0 = 3.8 grams]. This initial mass is modest even by the standards of Asian barbets, reflecting an altricial developmental strategy that necessitates intensive parental brooding and provisioning during the early nestling period. Incubation of the eggs, which lasts approximately 14.5 days [ab = approximately 14.5 days] at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], is a period of constant thermal maintenance that draws heavily on the attending adult's energetic reserves. This incubation duration, comparable to that reported for congeneric species such as Psilopogon lineatus, underscores the rapid embryogenesis typical of small-bodied piciform birds. The newly hatched chicks, entirely dependent on their parents for both warmth and food, must quickly gain mass to reach thermal independence and begin their development toward fledging.

Females of the Yellow-eared barbet ultimately attain an adult body mass averaging 33.3 grams [Wwi = 33.3 grams], with a documented range spanning 26 to 39 grams [Wwi = 26 to 39 grams] in field populations. This final mass represents a roughly ninefold increase from the hatchling stage, a growth trajectory that requires sustained high feeding rates throughout the nestling and fledgling periods. The species adheres to a single annual breeding cycle, with females typically laying a clutch of 2 to 4 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of 2 to 4 eggs] and producing one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. This modest reproductive output, combined with the extensive parental care demands, likely constrains the species to a relatively slow life-history pace compared to more fecund tropical passerines of similar body size.

Employing open-flow respirometry, researchers have measured the basal metabolic rate of adult Yellow-eared barbets and found a maximum oxygen consumption of 61.7 milliliters per hour [JOi = 61.7 milliliters per hour] when measured at the species' typical active body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This relatively high metabolic rate, characteristic of small-bodied endotherms with active foraging lifestyles, is energetically demanding and must be supported by a diet rich in fruits and insects. To meet these daily energetic costs, individuals spend a substantial portion of the daylight hours foraging. Under this same thermal regime of 41.8 °C, an entire suite of post-hatching developmental milestones unfolds: fledging from the nest occurs at 25 days after hatching [tx = 25 days after hatching], a point at which the chicks have acquired sufficient flight feather development to leave the cavity at a temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C].

The subsequent maturation period is extended relative to the nestling phase, with the young birds attaining sexual maturity at 75 days after hatching [tp = 75 days after hatching] under the same body temperature of 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C]. This delay between fledging and the attainment of reproductive capacity reflects the considerable time required for the full development of foraging skills, territory acquisition, and the physiological maturation of the gonads. Despite reaching sexual maturity at roughly two and a half months of age, the initiation of actual breeding is deferred even further. First successful reproduction is not typically observed until approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching] at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], a delay that suggests a period of social or logistical preparation before individuals enter the breeding population and secure a nesting territory.

Long-term banding studies have revealed that the Yellow-eared barbet exhibits a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 10.3 years [am = approximately 10.3 years] for individuals maintained at 41.8 °C [T = 41.8 °C], placing it among the longer-lived members of the Megalaimidae family given its moderate body size. This longevity is notable considering the energetic challenges posed by its high basal metabolic rate and the single annual reproductive event. The modest annual fecundity of 2 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 4 eggs per clutch] and a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] at that body temperature, paints a picture of a slow-paced, K-selected life history strategy. It is an adaptation likely tied to the stable, resource-limited environments of the lowland and foothill forests that Psilopogon australis inhabits across its Southeast Asian range.
